title: Sell Mineral Rights in Conecuh County, AL
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Conecuh County, AL
metaDescription: Own mineral or royalty interests in Conecuh County, Alabama? Get a hedged, activity-based cash offer for land near Evergreen, Castleberry, or Repton.
heroLead: Conecuh County sits on the flank of the Smackover-Norphlet trend that runs east from the old Citronelle discovery toward Jay Field, and the small legacy fields scattered through the county are the reason so many local families still hold minerals today.
intro: Conecuh County's oil and gas history is quieter than Mobile or Escambia County's, but it isn't thin. The McKenzie Field and several smaller Smackover and Norphlet prospects sit inside county lines or just across the border in Monroe and Escambia counties, and leasing swept through much of rural Conecuh during the mid-century boom years that followed the 1955 Citronelle discovery. A lot of that leasing never produced a well, which is exactly why owners here so often have a mineral interest sitting quietly in a family estate with no royalty history attached to it at all.

Piney Woods farmland, timber tracts, and small family homesteads make up most of the county, and the mineral estate under that land was frequently severed from the surface decades ago, sometimes during a timber sale, sometimes reserved in a will. We buy those interests directly, and this page covers how Conecuh County minerals are typically valued, what ownership tends to look like on the ground, and the questions owners ask most before deciding to sell.

sections.heading: Old leases and held-by-production questions
paragraphs: Because leasing in Conecuh County dates back decades in some places, a fair number of tracts carry an old lease that owners assume is still active. In most cases those leases lapsed long ago for lack of production or renewal, which restores full leasing rights to the mineral owner, but occasionally a lease was held by production from a small well that's still pumping quietly at a low rate.

Before we make an offer, we check the county's current well and permit status against any lease history in the courthouse abstract. If a well is actively producing on or near the tract, that materially changes the offer, since it means there's a real royalty stream to value rather than speculative acreage.

sections.heading: Heirs' property and the county courthouse
paragraphs: Conecuh County, like much of rural south Alabama, has a real heirs'-property pattern. Land passed down informally across generations, without a will or a clean estate settlement, ends up owned by dozens of cousins as tenants in common, each holding an undivided fractional share. It's common for a single mineral tract here to trace back to one grandparent whose estate was never formally probated, leaving the current generation without clear individual deeds to their share.

The Conecuh County Probate Court in Evergreen is the starting point for sorting that out. Whether the record shows a formal probate, an affidavit of heirship, or nothing at all beyond an old handwritten will, we work from whatever documentation exists and help identify what percentage a given family member actually owns before quoting a number.

sections.heading: What determines a fair range for a Conecuh County tract
paragraphs: We build a range from recent permit filings, any producing wells within the relevant spacing unit, and comparable lease bonus or purchase activity we track across the Smackover-Norphlet trend in south Alabama, rather than quoting a flat number for the whole county. A parcel near the McKenzie Field boundary carries a different range than acreage on the county's less-tested northern edge, and we'll explain which factors are driving the number we give you.

We won't promise a specific dollar figure per acre before reviewing the tract, and we won't call an offer guaranteed, because activity in this part of Alabama moves with commodity prices and drilling budgets that shift year to year.

sections.heading: Geology and the county's small legacy fields
paragraphs: Conecuh County lies along the eastern edge of the same Jurassic Smackover and Norphlet trend that produced the giant Citronelle Field to the west and Jay Field along the Florida line to the east. Between those two better-known fields, Conecuh has hosted smaller, scattered prospects, and permit activity here has always run in cycles tied to commodity prices rather than to any single sustained development program.

That pattern shapes how we look at value. A tract inside or near a historic field boundary, with documented well control nearby, is priced differently than acreage in an untested part of the county, and the honest answer for a given parcel usually depends on what the state's permit and production records show for that specific township and range.

faqs.question: My family's Conecuh County land was never formally probated. Can we still sell the minerals?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes, but every heir with a legal interest generally needs to be identified and sign off. We work from affidavits of heirship, old wills, or whatever partial documentation exists, and we'll walk you through what's needed to move forward.

faqs.question: There's an old lease on file for our land from decades ago. Is it still binding?
faqs.answer: Most leases from that era expired long ago if no well was drilled or production stopped, which returns full leasing rights to you. We check the current status against county and state permit records before making an offer so you know exactly where things stand.

faqs.question: How does Conecuh County compare to Mobile or Escambia County for mineral value?
faqs.answer: Conecuh generally sees less well control and thinner activity than the Citronelle or Jay Field cores, so ranges here tend to run lower, though tracts near the McKenzie Field or other documented prospects can still carry real value. We price against recent activity in your specific area rather than a countywide average.

faqs.question: Do you buy small fractional interests, like a sixteenth or a thirty-second?
faqs.answer: Yes. Fractional interests inherited across several generations are common in Conecuh County, and we regularly buy shares that small once ownership is documented.

faqs.question: What paperwork do I need before contacting you?
faqs.answer: A copy of any deed, will, or probate document you have is helpful, but not required to start. If you're unsure what you have, send what exists and we'll help sort out the ownership picture from there.
